description:
CS students, competing in person. We're building astronaut health monitoring software where every alert is based on NASA research, with a Mars mode for when Earth is too far away to help.

Skills: React, Node.js, Java, Python, ML, data analysis.

Looking for: a UI/UX designer, someone with a health or biology background, and a strong presenter.
summary:
Crew Health Check is an astronaut health-monitoring platform designed for missions where communication delays make immediate medical support from Earth impossible.

The platform enables astronauts to perform daily health check-ins and compares their readings against their individual in-flight baseline rather than relying solely on standard Earth-based thresholds. It identifies changes, visualizes health status through a colour-coded body map, and provides explainable alerts with recommended first steps.

Its key innovation is distance-aware decision support: the system considers communication delays across environments such as the International Space Station, the Moon and Mars to determine whether the crew should act onboard or consult medical teams on Earth.

The platform integrates three experimental AI models, including a solar particle event risk model trained on NASA space-weather data. AI insights are deliberately restricted from overriding safety decisions.

Crew Health Check demonstrates a transparent, explainable approach to astronaut health monitoring for future long-duration space missions.
details:
Overview

Crew Health Check is a browser-based astronaut health-monitoring and decision-support prototype developed by Team VoidShifters during NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

The project addresses a critical problem in long-duration human spaceflight: astronauts travelling beyond Earth cannot always depend on immediate medical assistance because communication delays increase significantly with distance.

How It Works

The platform provides a guided daily health check-in covering sleep, mood, symptoms, blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, blood glucose and exercise.

Instead of relying exclusively on conventional Earth-based reference ranges, the system compares new readings against each astronaut's individual in-flight baseline, built from their previous four weeks of readings.

It then provides:

  • A colour-coded body map showing Good, Watch or Act status.
  • Explainable alert cards describing what changed, why it matters and suggested first steps.
  • Distance-aware decision support that considers communication delays when determining whether the crew should act onboard or consult doctors on Earth.
  • Five mission environments: Space Station, Moon Base, Mars Transit, Mars Base and Mars Rover.
  • Personal health trends, 30-day charts and daily check-in streaks.
  • An Earth communication simulator that models message delays during space missions.
  • Body-area soreness reporting and simulated spacesuit skin sensors.

Three Experimental AI Models

The platform incorporates three AI models with deliberately restricted responsibilities.

Model 1 – Solar Particle Event Risk: Trained using NASA's DONKI space-weather records. It predicts whether solar flares may be followed by solar energetic particle events. It achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.900 on previously unseen test years, compared with 0.827 using flare class alone. It caught 49 of 59 relevant flares, with 207 false alarms. Its output is therefore labelled experimental and can only contribute a Watch-level insight.

Model 2 – Personal Pattern Detection: Uses an Isolation Forest-based approach to identify unusual combinations of health readings relative to an individual's baseline. It was evaluated on 900 simulated astronaut histories.

Model 3 – Earth Hospital Second Opinion: Developed using the PhysioNet 2019 clinical dataset containing 40,336 ICU patient records. It achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.617 on a separate hospital test set. Its output is restricted to an informational insight.

The underlying health rules, rather than AI predictions, control the actual health status and escalation decisions. Automated tests ensure that AI insights cannot override these decisions.

Innovation and Impact

The key innovation is the integration of personalized health monitoring with communication-delay-aware decision support.

A health event that can safely wait for Earth-based consultation in low Earth orbit may require immediate onboard action during a distant Mars mission. Crew Health Check demonstrates how mission location and response time can influence operational decision-making.

The project aims to support astronaut autonomy, improve situational awareness and contribute to safer future missions to the Moon and Mars.

Technology Stack

Frontend: React, TypeScript and Vite.

3D Visualization: Three.js and Blender.

Data Visualization: Recharts.

Machine Learning: Python and scikit-learn.

Deployment: Vercel.

Development: GitHub and Claude Code.

Development and Validation

The project was developed through an iterative milestone-based process during approximately 20 hours of hackathon development.

The development record includes 19 commits, more than 32,000 lines of TypeScript and Python, and 1,001 automated tests. The team also introduced 21 intentional faults during one testing milestone, all of which were detected by the tests.

Limitations

This is an experimental hackathon prototype, not a certified medical device. Health readings and astronaut profiles are simulated. The AI models have not been clinically validated for astronauts, and their outputs are not medical diagnoses or probabilities of illness. The 3D anatomical model is an in-progress component and is not yet part of the live application.
